<reason>Both sides were sharp and disciplined, but PRO kept a cleaner path to victory on the decisive clash: irreversibility and the ex ante default. CON's strongest thrusts — the "name the finding" fork, the "you rebuilt risk-based rules inside the licence" concession catch, the GDPR-architecture reversal, and the over-the-wire gap — all landed, but PRO answered each on the merits: the licence certifies a floor via burden-of-proof (failure to demonstrate = refusal), the motion's scope was staked in the opening ("the gate is the architecture"), and the chokepoint argument (B2.4) capped CON's proliferation point by locating the stakes in mass lawful deployment, which CON's regime leaves open pre-release. Crucially, CON never squarely answered PRO's Q2 — what stops a dangerous frontier model entering the EU market — retreating to "neither regime stops the wire," which concedes the lawful channel PRO's gate governs. CON's fallback claim that the status quo already runs ex ante authority verification was shaky against the self-assessment reality PRO pressed. Both Rebuttal 2s answered A1/A2 properly; both sides had one clipped turn, roughly symmetric. CON's closing rhetorically mirrored PRO's final line well but repeated the over-the-wire point without engaging the chokepoint answer.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's B2.4 chokepoint reversal ("lawful market access is the channel where harm scales; a rogue download is a law-enforcement problem under any regime") combined with B3.2's question and B4.5-B4.6 pressing CON's failure to name any ex ante stop — it defined the winning clash and CON never closed that hole.</best_rebuttal>
